item.title: Nazi-looted Kandinsky from Amsterdam family sold for almost €32m
item.description:
Nazi-looted Kandinsky from Amsterdam family sold for almost €32m

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A painting by Wassily Kandinsky looted from a Jewish family in Amsterdam has sold at Christie’s in London for £27 million, (€32 million), broadcaster NOS reported.

Kandinsky painted Das bunte Leben (The colourful life) in Paris in 1907. Emanuel and Hedwig Lewenstein, who ran a sewing machine factory on the Dam, bought it in 1927. Their collection also included works by Jan Toorop, Jozef Israëls, and Jean Metzinger.

The painting was auctioned shortly after the German occupation began and was bought by Jewish collector Sal Slijper. His family later sold it to the Bayerische Landesbank, which loaned it permanently to the Lenbachhaus museum in Munich, where it hung for decades.

Researchers found that in 1940 a museum employee, acting for an unknown person, had the work taken to the auction house by courier. They said there were many indications the Nazis had seized it.

In 2023, the German public prosecution department classified the painting as looted art and the bank returned it to the Lewensteins’ heirs.

That same year, the heirs sold another Kandinsky, Bild mit Häusern, for more than €60 million. Amsterdam city council returned that work after a years-long dispute. It had hung in the Stedelijk Museum until February 2022.

item.title: Thousands of women abused in postwar Dutch camps, study finds
item.description:
Thousands of women abused in postwar Dutch camps, study finds

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A study released Thursday by the NIOD Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies has found that thousands of women imprisoned in internment camps after World War II were systematically sexually abused but that evidence of the crimes was hidden away.

The women, who were accused of having relationships with Germans during the Occupation of the Netherlands or were suspected collaborators, were subjected to “rapes, sadistic torture, forced undressing and public humiliations” in dozens of the country’s more than 200 internment camps, said NIOD.

Some 200 victims and witnesses gave statements to then-retired police inspector Johanna van Schilfgaarde for parliament’s 1950 Committee of Inquiry, but their accounts never made it into the final report.

Lead researcher at the time, Arnaud Baron van Tuyll van Serooskerken, was appointed to investigate reports of camp abuses, but concluded he couldn’t finish his assignment because witnesses were too afraid to speak out.

But the women’s testimonies were indeed in the archives, with almost all of them reporting sexual abuse and sadistic abuse by camp guards, including rape and sexual assault.

“In dozens of internment camps, structural sexual violence has been used by guards,” said historian and journalist Ewoud Kieft, who conducted the research for NIOD. “The lead investigator was grossly negligent, he told broadcaster NOS. “He failed to do his job.”

Because the committee’s final report contained no reference to the women’s testimonies, the Dutch government was never held to account.

Sixteen internment camp officials were eventually punished for murders and torture and were given fines or one-year prison sentences, but no one is known to have been punished for rape and sexual violence against women.

Kieft calls the testimonies “the tip of the iceberg” and has vowed to continue his research.

item.title: No Picnic: inquiry reveals Dutch cycling team’s toxic culture
item.description:
No Picnic: inquiry reveals Dutch cycling team’s toxic culture

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch cycling team Picnic-PostNL has been silently struggling with an oppressive atmosphere and culture of intimidation, according to an investigation published by broadcaster NOS and cycling platform In De Waaier.

Many of the team’s former members have been left traumatised and described a “culture of fear” and “unsafe working conditions”.

Reporters confidentially spoke with 71 current and former employees of the team, which competes in the World Tour, the sport’s top division. It currently employs around 120 people. Many people described how management would punish criticism and ignore mental health complaints.

One interviewee described the management structure as a “dictatorship” and another said team members were treated as “puppets”.

This began after the team’s successes in the Tour de France in 2013 and 2014, when German rider Marcel Kittel won stages as a sprinter. After that, the managers became paranoid about losing control of the team, one person told NOS.

More rules were established and people were told “everyone is replaceable.”

After Dutch racer Tom Dumoulin won the 2017 Giro d’Italia, one of cycling’s three Grand Tours, the managers became even more “radicalised”, according to another interviewee.

Dutch rider Martijn Tusveld described how he was dropped from major races for questioning the team’s tactics. He became so anxious he considered harming himself. He left the team and said he is still mentally unwell.

Another, who was suffering mentally, said he was told by sports director Rudi Kemna “I don’t believe in psychologists” after he asked for help.

The Dutch professional cyclists’ association VVBW told NOS it had heard similar accounts over the past 18 months, with some riders calling in tears.

NOS has asked the team owner Iwan Spekenbrink for a comment but he has so far refused to reply to any allegations in person or in writing.

item.title: MPs move to curb small schools amid cost and curricula concerns
item.description:
MPs move to curb small schools amid cost and curricula concerns

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

MPs and the cabinet want to curb the growth of small, independent schools in the Netherlands, after a school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) opened with just four pupils, according to broadcaster NOS.

A 2021 law made it easier to set up state-funded schools based on new educational ideas or on religious or other “worldview” beliefs. Since then, more schools have opened every year, a large share of them Islamic.

The “Renaissance School” in Almere, which opened in August, was approved partly on the basis of market research showing around 350 people were positive about it.

MPs from both coalition and opposition parties said the research amounted to little more than an online survey, and that respondents often did not know what kind of school was planned. It is linked to the far-right FVD party.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen told parliament on Wednesday she would look at whether that part of the law should be tightened or scrapped. She had already written to MPs that keeping so many small schools going was “no longer sustainable”.

Tielen said she saw no reason to intervene at the Renaissance School for now. It must have at least 139 pupils by the start of its fourth school year or close.

The law originally was a VVD initiative, which the FVD voted against it at the time.

The debate comes a year after research by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur found that a number of orthodox Protestant and Islamic schools were teaching messages at odds with democratic values, such as rejecting same-sex relationships or teaching that women should be subordinate to men.

All schools in the Netherlands are legally required to stick to democratic values, including equality and non-discrimination. The schools inspectorate said it would investigate where necessary.

item.title: Dronten wreckage identified as British WWII bomber
item.description:
Dronten wreckage identified as British WWII bomber

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Aircraft wreckage uncovered four years ago in Dronten has been identified as a British WWII bomber, according to local officials.

Discovered in what is now the Van Veldhuizenbos forest in Dronten, the aircraft is said to be a British Avro Lancaster Mk III that was shot down by German forces on the night of September 27-28, 1943, while attempting to target Hanover, Germany.

The aircraft, run by the Canadian 405 Pathfinder Squadron stationed near Cambridge, England, crashed into what was then the Ijsselmeer.

The plane was carrying seven crew members – four Canadians, one Australian, and two Britons – whose bodies were never recovered. But human remains were found in 1959 and buried in the Jonkerbos War Cemetery in Nijmegen.

Additional human remains were discovered and are now being examined by the Ministry of Defence’s Recovery and Identification Service to see if they belong to the slain crew members.

“Behind every plane wreck lies a human story,” said Dronten mayor Jean Paul Gebben, who said the aircraft’s identification was of great historical significance.

Some of the recovered wreckage will be loaned to museums and foundations.

The government estimates that some 5,500 aircraft were lost over the Netherlands during the Second World War. Annually, a maximum of three aircraft recovery operations are carried out in the country, with the costs mostly covered by the national government.

item.title: Police urge Ahold to file a report over cybersecurity breach
item.description:
Police urge Ahold to file a report over cybersecurity breach

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch police and the Public Prosecutors Office have asked Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Albert Heijn, to file a report on what the company is still calling a “cybersecurity incident”.

“There is currently no criminal investigation into the incident,” the police said in a press release issued on Wednesday. “Police and the OM have been in contact with Ahold Delhaize. The company has been invited to file a report.”

“In order to successfully track down and prosecute, it is crucial to always get information from victims as quickly as possible.”

Although Ahold did report the incident, which began on Sunday night, to the National Cyber Security Centre as required by law, a criminal investigation can’t be started without a formal police report.

The company says it will “work with all relevant authorities”, but it gave no explanation as to why it hasn’t filed a report and said it is not currently making any further statements.

The incident hit other Ahold chains Etos and Gall & Gall, leading the company to shut down several of its IT systems that has continued to make online shopping and deliveries impossible.

Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad, on condition of anonymity, that the crisis is costing Ahold Delhaize “tens of millions” of euros a day. Ahold told the paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

Fresh produce took a particularly hard hit, with the supermarkets’ fruit and vegetable sections very low on stock.

Albert Heijn said on Thursday that its distribution centres are running again, but its website and delivery services are still not operating, meaning customers still can’t place orders online or via app. Deliveries of fresh products were also said to be resuming as of Thursday night, while delivery of non-perishable products has been fully restored.

“This is a positive step forward in the recovery of our supply chain,” said the company. “The investigation into the nature and cause of the cybersecurity incident is ongoing. At this time, there is no indication that any customer or employee data has been involved in the incident.”

Bad actors

“We can no longer see cybercrime as a collection of separate crimes, but as a criminal ecosystem,” said a police statement. “Behind almost every attack lies a chain of cooperating perpetrators, resources and criminal services that reinforce each other: a criminal supply chain.”

Several foreign servers are known to be used in the attack, including in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that’s where the attacks are coming from as traffic can be routed through other countries.

Ahold supermarkets in Belgium (Delhaize) and the US (Stop & Shop and Food Lion) have also been affected.

The Albert Heijn incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France.

item.title: Dutch cabinet wants AI to help slash civil service: Telegraaf
item.description:
Dutch cabinet wants AI to help slash civil service: Telegraaf

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet is planning to slash the civil service with the help of new AI technologies, which could save hundreds of millions of euros, the Telegraaf reported on Thursday.

Sources told the paper that Eric van der Burg, the VVD junior home affairs minister, will soon present targets for cutting staff numbers, although estimates are not yet known.

Experts told the Telegraaf the rise in civil servants, which went from 140,000 in 2021 to 170,000 last year, that things are not improving. One said the government is being stifled with ever more rules and subsidies.

Policy officials in particular, who have almost doubled to 20,000 in the past decade, are putting needless pressure on the government, one analyst said.

Insiders said using AI could save an extra €200 million in both 2028 and 2029. A further €200 million has been planned for the interior ministry’s budget for the following year, rising to €1 billion a year from 2035.

Van der Burg is reported to be partly following the thinking of an advisory committee on the future of the civil service, which is due to present conclusions this year.

Ahead of a meeting with MPs, the committee said digitalisation and AI can make government more efficient, but only if the build-up of rules and checks is also tackled.

Government economist Jos Blank wrote that the state had been underperforming for decades, and that a constant stream of new rules, subsidies and mergers was making public services worse.

Former senior civil servant Roel Bekker criticised growing “policy overload” and called for the number of policy officials to be cut by 20% to 30%.

item.title: Unemployment remains at 4%, 408,000 out of work
item.description:
Unemployment remains at 4%, 408,000 out of work

October 15, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Over 408,000 people were out of work in September, national statistics office CBS said on Thursday.

The number of jobless people rose by an average of 5,000 a month over the past three months. The number of people in paid work stayed level.

Unemployment returned to 4% in July after dipping slightly in June. A year ago, 409,000 people were out of work, also 4% of the workforce.

The recent rise is mainly down to fewer unemployed people finding work rather than people losing their jobs.

Benefits agency UWV was paying out 197,100 unemployment benefits at the end of September. The UWV figures are not directly comparable with the CBS total, which counts everyone without paid work who is actively looking for a job.

A further 3.2 million people aged 15 to 75 are not counted as part of the workforce because they have not recently looked for work or cannot start straight away. Most are retired or unable to work because of illness or disability.

item.title: Hadj Moussa sinks Como as Feyenoord claim first CL group win
item.description:
Hadj Moussa sinks Como as Feyenoord claim first CL group win

October 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord claimed the first win for the Eredivisie teams in the Champions League as they got the better of Italian upstarts Como 1907 in a five-goal thriller.

After a cagey opening, Como took the lead when Assane Diao won a physical challenge on the left with Javi Lopez and drilled the ball past Tjark Ernst from a tight angle.

Feyenoord were level within two minutes as Gjivai Zechiël span away from his marker on the edge of the penalty area and lofted a shot into the top corner.

The visitors suffered a setback when Diao limped off a few minutes later, while Feyenoord grew in confidence, with Givairo Read and Lopez drawing fingertip saves from Como goalkeeper Robert Sanchez just before half-time.

Feyenoord went ahead with the first real chance after the interval, as Anis Haji Moussa cut in from the right and found the bottom corner of Sanchez’ net.

Ten minutes from the end the Algerian appeared to have put the result beyond doubt when his long-range shot came back off the post and deflected in off the goalkeeper’s back to make the score 3-1.

Tasos Douvikas’s injury-time strike for Como ensured a tense last few minutes, but Feyenoord were not to be denied.

Zechiël said the quick reply after Diao put the visitors ahead was crucial for his teammates’ morale. “That gave the team and the stadium the feeling we were going to win today.”

He was full of praise for Hadj Moussa, who had a decisive role in both second-half goals. “Anis is a top-class player. We’re really pleased that he’s still available for us this season.”

The result lifts Feyenoord to 23rd place in the 36-team table, while their next match is a trip to Real Betis next Wednesday, October 21.

item.title: Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
item.description:
Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law

October 14, 2026 Louis Gore-Langton

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Highly skilled workers, students and family migrants will no longer be entitled to penalty payments when the immigration service IND misses its deadlines, the asylum ministry has said after a new law was passed by the senate on Tuesday.

The change was presented as an asylum measure, but a ministry spokesperson told Dutch News the law applies to applications for all regular residence permits.

The IND is supposed to make a decision on a residence application within 6 months. If it misses that deadline, applicants can go to court to demand a payment for every day it remains late. Once the new law takes effect, judges will only be able to order the IND to reach a decision within a set period.

The government abandoned plans to axe penalty payments for regular residence applicants in 2024, saying it could conflict with EU law. The ministry told us it could not yet say what had changed.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink told MPs in September the IND had paid out close to €100 million in penalties, noting that some asylum applicants had ended up receiving over €100,000. The IND also insists these penalties do nothing to speed things up.

A spokesperson from the IND told Dutch News the service does not currently know how much in penalty payments is paid for regular permit applicants, but it will calculate the figures in the coming weeks.

D66, which voted against the asylum package in April, backed the new law. In April, D66 senator Boris Dittrich told Dutch News the party opposed the package because it would have made living in the country without valid papers a criminal offence. That measure is not part of the new law.

A D66 spokesperson acknowledged that the IND’s failure to meet deadlines “is not resolved by this amendment”, but told us on Tuesday the penalties “no longer provide an incentive to work more efficiently and have therefore outlived their purpose”.

“In our view, abolishing the penalty payments must go hand in hand with measures aimed at the ultimate goal: faster procedures, so that everyone who comes here receives clarity as quickly as possible,” the spokesperson said.
